title: The Completion Drop

scenario.situation: Course completion fell from 58% to 43% after quizzes were added to modules.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The content lead assumes the quizzes are driving learners away and wants them removed.
scenario.question: Are the quizzes actually causing learners to drop off?

decisions.prompt: The content lead wants the quizzes pulled. How do you frame your investigation?

options.label: A/B comparison of quiz vs. no-quiz courses
options.detail: Compare completion rates on courses that have quizzes to those that don't.
options.consequence: You find quiz courses do have lower completion — but quiz and non-quiz courses may differ in difficulty, length, and audience. The comparison is confounded before you start.
options.divergenceCost: Compared non-equivalent course populations, baking in confounds.

options.label: Metric audit before trend reading
options.detail: Ask whether 'completion' means the same thing before and after the change, then examine engagement and pass-through rates as a counterfactual.
options.consequence: You discover that 'completed' was redefined when quizzes shipped — it now requires passing them. The old and new numbers are not the same metric. The investigation resets on solid ground.

options.label: Learner exit survey
options.detail: Survey learners who stopped mid-course to ask why they left.
options.consequence: You collect anecdotes — many mention quizzes — but the sample skews toward vocal leavers, and you still don't know whether overall engagement actually fell.
options.divergenceCost: Chose a slow, biased instrument that amplifies complaints without confirming a real drop.

options.label: Time-series regression on completion rate
options.detail: Model completion rate over time, flagging the quiz launch as an intervention.
options.consequence: The model confirms a drop at the launch date — but it assumes the metric was consistent across that date, which it wasn't. You've quantified an artifact, not a behavior change.
options.divergenceCost: Modeled a break that was definitional, not behavioral — garbage-in, garbage-out.

decisions.prompt: You suspect the definition may have changed. Which metric do you use to assess whether learner engagement actually dropped?

artifact.title: Completion rate before vs. after quiz launch (official metric)
artifact.caption: The headline number looks like a 15-point drop — but both bars carry the label 'completion rate.' Do they measure the same thing?

options.label: Official completion rate (pre vs. post)
options.detail: Use the reported completion figures to quantify the decline and its magnitude.
options.consequence: The 15-point gap looks damning — but pre-launch 'complete' meant finishing the last lesson, and post-launch it means passing quizzes too. You are comparing apples to oranges under the same label.
options.divergenceCost: Trusted a metric that silently changed definition — read a measurement artifact as a real trend.

options.label: Last-lesson reach rate (definition-stable metric)
options.detail: Measure the share of enrolled learners who reached the final lesson in both periods — a definition that holds constant across the change.
options.consequence: Under a stable definition, last-lesson reach is 56% pre-launch and 54% post-launch — statistically flat. The dramatic 'drop' was entirely an artifact of the redefined metric, not a behavior change.

artifact.title: Last-lesson reach rate before vs. after quiz launch (definition-stable)
artifact.caption: Holding the definition constant, reach is virtually unchanged. The 15-point gap was a measurement artifact, not a learner behavior shift.

decisions.prompt: The definition-stable metric shows no real drop. What do you tell the content lead?

options.label: "The quizzes have no effect — keep them and don't worry."
options.detail: Declare the quizzes exonerated and close the investigation.
options.consequence: You've correctly identified a measurement artifact but overclaimed the conclusion. The stable reach rate rules out a mass dropout, but it doesn't prove quizzes are harmless — some friction may still exist at smaller scale.
options.divergenceCost: Overclaimed a null effect from evidence that only ruled out one hypothesis.

options.label: "The drop is a metric redefinition artifact, not a behavior change — but let's track quiz-attempt and pass rates to confirm quizzes aren't adding friction."
options.detail: Report the finding, flag the measurement issue, and propose a forward-looking monitoring plan.
options.consequence: You reframe the content lead's assumption with evidence, surface a data-quality issue that will recur if unaddressed, and recommend the next measurement step. The quizzes aren't condemned or fully cleared — they're under proper watch.

insight: The completion drop was not caused by quizzes deterring learners — it was caused by a silent redefinition of 'complete' that made the pre- and post-launch numbers incomparable. Under a definition-stable metric, learner reach was flat. The lesson is metric definition stability: before reading any trend, confirm the metric means the same thing at every point in the series. A number with a changing definition is not a time series — it is two different measurements wearing the same name.
